html:
The map's label for the peoples of mainland Australia, who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, shown from 2000 BCE to 1815. Their history as a whole is told in Aboriginal Australian societies.

Their ancestors arrived from the north at least 50,000 years ago. Burials at Lake Mungo, such as Mungo Man, are around 40,000 years old. By the time of British settlement there were several hundred nations and more than 250 languages. Each people belonged to its own Country, with laws, songs and stories held in what English speakers call the Dreaming.

This was not a simple life of wandering. People managed the land:

  • they burned country in planned patterns, fire-stick farming, to renew grass and draw game;
  • at Budj Bim in the southeast the Gunditjmara built stone channels and traps to farm eels, thousands of years old;
  • in the inland they ground grass seeds into flour, among the oldest seed grinding in the world;
  • trade routes carried ochre, stone axes and shells across the continent.

The dingo arrived about 3,500 years ago, brought by seafarers. From the 1700s Makassan trepang fishers from Sulawesi visited the northern coast every year.

The First Fleet landed at Sydney Cove in 1788. Smallpox swept through the people of the Sydney region the next year, and as settlement spread, land was taken and many were killed on the frontier.
